steps.body: Right triangles cap θ below 90° — the unit circle removes the cap. Draw a circle of radius 1 and rotate a point θ from the positive x-axis: **cos θ is the point's x-coordinate, sin θ is its y-coordinate.** For acute θ this reproduces the old ratios (hypotenuse 1) — but now EVERY angle, any size, any sign, has a sine and cosine.
Spin the angle and watch the point trace the circle. The two colored legs are exactly cos θ and sin θ — swing past 90° and watch cos slip negative.

widget.prompt: Drag the angle to 120° and read the coordinates.
widget.successFeedback: At 120° the point is (cos 120°, sin 120°) ≈ (−0.5, 0.866): cos is negative in Quadrant II, sin still positive.
widget.lowFeedback: Not far enough — keep rotating counterclockwise toward 120°, up and over the top of the circle.
widget.highFeedback: Past 120° now — rotate back clockwise. Watch how crossing an axis flips a coordinate's sign.

predict.prompt: You'll rotate from 0° to 120°. What does the point's HEIGHT do along the way?
predict.reveal: The height rises until the top of the circle at 90°, then falls — the sine's peak is exactly where the point is highest.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents tf unit circle.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for tf unit circle must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines tf unit circle.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

steps.body: Read the top of the circle.

widget.prompt: At 90° the rotating point sits at the circle's very top, (0, 1). What is sin 90°?

commonErrors.feedback: 0 is the X-coordinate — that's cos 90°. Sine reads the y-coordinate: 1.
90 is the angle, not its sine. The sine is the point's HEIGHT on the unit circle: 1.

explanationVariants: At 180° the point sits at (−1, 0), so cos 180° = x = −1.
Half a turn points straight LEFT — the x-coordinate is as negative as it gets.

widget.prompt: At 180° the point sits at (−1, 0). What is cos 180°?

commonErrors.feedback: The point is on the LEFT half of the circle — its x-coordinate is negative: cos 180° = −1.
0 is the y-coordinate — that's sin 180°. Cosine reads x: −1.

steps.body: Signs now come free from the QUADRANT. Q1: x and y both positive — everything positive. Q2: x < 0 — only sine positive. Q3: both negative — only tangent (y/x) positive. Q4: y < 0 — only cosine positive. The classic mnemonic, counterclockwise from Q1: **A-S-T-C** — All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine.

widget.prompt: Sort each value by its sign — no calculator, just the quadrant.

items.label: sin 200°
items.feedback: 200° lands in Q3, below the x-axis — y is negative, so sine is negative.

items.label: cos 100°
items.feedback: 100° is Q2, left of the y-axis — x is negative, so cosine is negative.

items.label: sin 100°
items.feedback: Q2 sits ABOVE the x-axis — y stays positive, and Q2 is exactly the S of A-S-T-C.

items.label: cos 320°
items.feedback: 320° is Q4, right of the y-axis — x is positive, the C quadrant of A-S-T-C.

widget.missFeedback: Place the angle in its quadrant, then read the sign of the coordinate the function uses.
widget.successFeedback: A-S-T-C sorted — quadrant first, sign for free.

explanationVariants: Q3 sits left of the y-axis AND below the x-axis — x < 0 and y < 0, so sine and cosine are both negative.
That's why Q3 is the T of A-S-T-C: only y/x, two negatives, comes out positive.

widget.prompt: In which quadrant are sin θ AND cos θ both negative?

options.label: Quadrant III
options.feedback: Right — both coordinates go negative only in the lower left, which is what makes tan = y/x positive there.

options.label: Quadrant II
options.feedback: Q2 has x < 0 but the point is still ABOVE the axis — sine stays positive (the S quadrant).

options.label: Quadrant IV
options.feedback: Q4 has y < 0 but x > 0 — cosine stays positive (the C quadrant).

options.label: Quadrant I
options.feedback: Q1 is the A quadrant — everything is positive there.

steps.body: Tangent rides along: **tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = y/x** — the SLOPE of the radius line. Its sign follows the quadrant rules, and it has a failure mode the others don't: wherever x = 0 (straight up at 90°, straight down at 270°), the division breaks.

options.label: Undefined — the point is (0, 1), and y/x divides by zero
options.feedback: Exactly — a vertical radius has no slope. Tangent breaks at 90° and 270°, wherever x = 0.
1 is tan 45°, where x and y balance. At 90° the x-coordinate is ZERO and the division breaks.
Tangent is 0 where the Y-coordinate is 0 (at 0° and 180°). At 90° it's the x that vanishes — undefined.
That feeds the angle back as the answer — tan 90° asks for y/x at (0, 1), which has no value.

explanationVariants: At 270° the point is (0, −1): sin 270° = y = −1.
Three-quarters of a turn points straight DOWN — height as negative as possible.

commonErrors.feedback: 270° points straight DOWN, to (0, −1) — the height is −1, not +1 (that's 90°, the top).
0 is the x-coordinate — cos 270°. Sine reads the height: −1.

hints: 270° is three quarter-turns — the point at the circle's bottom.

takeaways: Unit circle: cos θ = x, sin θ = y — every angle now has values.
A-S-T-C gives each quadrant's positive function; coordinates explain why.
tan = y/x, the radius's slope — undefined where x = 0 (90°, 270°).
steps.teaser: Next: reference angles — how the whole circle recycles Quadrant I's values.

concept.body: Start at the start. At 0° the point hasn't rotated at all — it sits at (1, 0) on the positive x-axis. So cos 0° = x = 1 and sin 0° = y = 0. Every unit-circle read is just this: find the point, read the coordinate.

explanationVariants: Full width right, zero height — cosine 1, sine 0.

widget.prompt: At 0° the point sits at (1, 0). What is cos 0°?

commonErrors.feedback: 0 is the y-coordinate — sin 0°. Cosine reads x: 1.
−1 is the point at 180°, on the far LEFT. At 0° the x-coordinate is +1.
